teaser: Stone that weighs nearly three times as much as water, carved until it looks like warm skin.
review_notes:
Catalog year is 1817; the Hermitage version is usually dated 1813-1816, and 1814-1817 is the date of the second version (V&A / National Galleries of Scotland). The lesson avoids contradicting the catalog but mentions both versions.
Height given as about 1.82 m (Hermitage version).
Canova finishing the surface himself, sometimes by candlelight, and toning the marble with a light wash: widely reported, wording kept general.
Hermitage acquisition in 1901 from the Leuchtenberg collection: please confirm.
Second version bought jointly in 1994 for 7.6 million pounds: please confirm the figure.
Which hand belongs to which Grace is hard to read in the photo; spot texts stay deliberately neutral.

lesson.text: Marble is rock. A bucket of it weighs almost three times as much as the same bucket filled with water, and it is cold enough to chill your palm. This group stands about 1.82 meters tall (roughly 6 feet), so you are facing several hundred kilos of stone. Nothing in it looks heavy.

The three women are the Graces of Greek myth, daughters of Zeus: Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia. They stood for beauty, joy and abundance, the gifts that make life pleasant rather than merely possible. Artists had shown them for two thousand years, nearly always the same way.

In the ancient formula, the Graces stand in a row and the middle one turns her back to you. Antonio Canova broke the row. He pulled the three sisters into a huddle, face to face, so that the subject is no longer three beautiful bodies. It is what happens between them.
Follow the arms first. They do the work a frame would do in a painting.

lines.label: The ring
lines.text: Heads, shoulders and arms close into a loop. Your eye circles inside it and has no reason to leave. Three people become one shape.

lines.label: Three faces, one line
lines.text: The two outer sisters look toward the one in the middle, who lowers her eyes. The heads nearly touch: the distance of a secret.

lines.label: The sway
lines.text: Each body bends in a soft S, weight on one leg, the other relaxed. This ancient stance is called contrapposto, and it keeps a standing figure from looking like a post.

lesson.text: That ring is why the group never feels static, even though nobody moves. Canova wanted you to walk around it, and from each side a different sister comes forward. The photo you are seeing is only one of many possible views.
The first buyer never saw it finished. Joséphine, Napoleon's former wife and a devoted collector of Canova, ordered the group in 1812 and died in 1814 while the marble was still in his Roman studio.

Her son Eugène claimed the statue, and his own son later carried it to Russia when he married a daughter of the tsar. That is how three Greek goddesses carved in Rome for a French empress ended up in the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg, where the museum acquired them in 1901.

Now, the surface. Canova's assistants roughed out the block using measuring points taken from his full-size plaster model. The last layer, the one that counts, he kept for himself. Go and see what that last layer does.

lesson.title: Stone turned to skin
lesson.text: Four places where marble behaves like something else.

spots.title: Fingers at the cheek
spots.text: A hand comes up to the middle sister's face, fingers barely resting on it. Canova carves a touch so light that you sense no pressure at all.

spots.title: Arm on flesh
spots.text: Where the long arm crosses a chest, the stone seems to give slightly, the way a body does when it is held. That softness is pure illusion.

spots.title: The single cloth
spots.text: One strip of drapery winds between the three and hangs in deep folds. Its busy creases make the smooth skin beside it look even smoother.

spots.title: The garlanded pillar
spots.text: Behind the left sister, a small altar hung with flowers. It is also engineering: it helps brace six slender legs that carry all that marble.

lesson.text: Did you spot the thin gray lines running through the thighs? Those are natural veins in the marble. No sculptor can see inside a block before cutting it, so every figure carries a little of the quarry's luck.

An English duke fell for the group in Canova's studio and tried to buy it. Refused, he ordered a second one for his country house. In 1994 that version was bought jointly by two British museums, in London and Edinburgh, for 7.6 million pounds.

Canova worked in a style called Neoclassicism: a return to the calm, clear forms of ancient Greece and Rome after a century of ornate decoration. Some later viewers found his goddesses too polished, almost sugary. The polish was the point. He wanted an ideal, not a portrait.
To take the glare off freshly cut marble, Canova is reported to have toned his statues with a faint wash, and to have checked the last polishing by candlelight, where every bump throws a shadow.
Canova's idea was simple and new: turn the three Graces toward each other. The beauty he shows is not in any one body but in the closed circle of their affection.

quiz.question: How did ancient artists usually arrange the three Graces?
options: In a row, the middle one seen from behind
Dancing far apart from each other
quiz.explanation: Canova broke that old row and turned all three toward each other.

quiz.question: Who ordered this group but died before it was finished?
quiz.explanation: Joséphine commissioned it in 1812 and died in 1814.

quiz.question: What does contrapposto mean?
options: A stance with the weight on one leg, giving the body a soft S curve
quiz.explanation: It is the relaxed, swaying stance borrowed from ancient statues.

quiz.question: What is the small garlanded pillar behind the figures also useful for?
options: Helping to support the heavy group
quiz.explanation: It braces the slender legs that carry the marble.

quiz.question: What are the thin gray lines visible on the legs?
quiz.explanation: They are veins in the stone that no sculptor can foresee.

facts.text: Canova's assistants did the rough carving, and he finished the surface himself.
facts.explanation: The lesson explains that he kept the final layer for his own hand.

facts.text: Only one version of The Three Graces exists.
facts.explanation: An English duke ordered a second version, now shared by museums in London and Edinburgh.

facts.text: Neoclassicism looked back to the art of ancient Greece and Rome.
facts.explanation: It was a return to calm, clear ancient forms after a century of ornate decoration.
